Coconut Fish Curry with Lime and Lemongrass
Ingredients:

For the Curry:

1 lb white fish fillets (e.g., cod, tilapia, or snapper), cut into chunks

1 tbsp lime juice

1 tsp salt

2 tbsp vegetable oil

1 onion, finely chopped

2 garlic cloves, minced

1-inch piece of ginger, grated

2 stalks lemongrass, bruised and cut into 2-inch pieces

1-2 Thai red chilies, finely sliced (adjust to taste)

2 tsp turmeric powder

1 tsp ground coriander

1 (14 oz) can coconut milk

½ cup water or fish stock

1 tbsp fish sauce

1 tsp sugar (optional)

4-5 kaffir lime leaves (optional, for extra aroma)

Zest and juice of 1 lime

Preparation:

Marinate the Fish:

In a bowl, toss the fish chunks with 1 tablespoon lime juice and 1 teaspoon salt. Set aside to marinate for about 10 minutes.

Sauté the Aromatics:

In a large pot or deep skillet, heat 2 tablespoons of vegetable oil over medium heat.

Add the chopped onion and sauté for 3-4 minutes until softened.

Add the minced garlic, grated ginger, and sliced Thai red chilies. Stir and cook for another 1-2 minutes until fragrant.

Add Spices and Liquids:

Stir in the turmeric powder and ground coriander, cooking for about 30 seconds to release the flavors.

Pour in the coconut milk and water (or fish stock). Stir to combine.

Add the bruised lemongrass stalks, kaffir lime leaves (if using), fish sauce, and sugar (optional). Bring the curry to a simmer and cook for 5-7 minutes to let the spices infuse.

Cook the Fish:

Carefully add the marinated fish chunks into the curry, gently stirring to ensure the fish is covered in the sauce.

Let the curry simmer for 8-10 minutes, or until the fish is cooked through and tender. The fish should easily flake with a fork.

Finish the Curry:

Remove the curry from heat and discard the lemongrass stalks and kaffir lime leaves.

Stir in the lime zest and juice to brighten the flavors. Taste the curry and adjust the seasoning with more salt, fish sauce, or lime juice if needed.

WANANCHI WA PWANI: HAKI ZENU, WAJIBU WENU, NA MUSTAKABALI WA PWANI
Pwani imebarikiwa kwa rasilimali nyingi kuliko maeneo mengi nchini Kenya. Tuna bahari, bandari, ardhi yenye rutuba, utalii, gesi, chumvi, samaki, na nafasi ya kipekee ya kijiografia. Lakini kwa miaka mingi, wananchi wa Pwani wameendelea kuishi katika umasikini, ukosefu wa ajira, migogoro ya ardhi na maendeleo duni. Swali ni: ni nani wa kulaumiwa?
Jibu ni moja kwa moja: viongozi wabovu na wananchi waliokosa kuwawajibisha.
1️⃣ ARDHI: JERAHA LA MUDA MREFU PWANI
Pwani ndiyo eneo lenye migogoro mingi ya ardhi Kenya.
Maelfu ya wananchi hawana hatimiliki
Ardhi ya mababu imechukuliwa na wachache wenye nguvu
Vijana wamegeuzwa vibarua kwenye ardhi yao wenyewe
Wananchi wana jukumu la:
Kudai hatimiliki kupitia kaunti na serikali kuu
Kuwahoji viongozi waliokaa ofisini miaka 5–10 bila kutatua migogoro ya ardhi
Kukataa kura kwa viongozi wanaotumia ardhi kama ahadi ya kampeni lakini hawatekelezi
👉 Hakuna maendeleo bila haki ya ardhi.
2️⃣ BANDARI YA MOMBASA: UTAJIRI USIOFAIDISHA WENYEJI
Bandari ya Mombasa ni lango la uchumi wa Afrika Mashariki, ikikusanya mabilioni ya shilingi kila mwaka.
Lakini:
Vijana wa Pwani hawapati ajira za maana
Ajira nyingi huenda kwa watu kutoka nje ya Pwani
Maamuzi hufanywa Nairobi bila kushirikisha wenyeji
Wananchi wana wajibu wa:
Kudai sera ya ajira kwa wenyeji (local content)
Kuhoji wabunge na maseneta wao: Bandari imesaidiaje vijana wa Pwani?
Kukataa viongozi wanaotetea bandari lakini hawatetee ajira za watu wao
👉 Bandari bila ajira kwa wenyeji ni unyonyaji, si maendeleo.
3️⃣ AJIRA: VIJANA PWANI WAMECHOSHWA
Pwani ina kiwango kikubwa cha ukosefu wa ajira kwa vijana.
Elimu ipo, lakini nafasi hakuna
Ujuzi upo, lakini upendeleo nao upo
Serikali za kaunti zimekuwa mashine za kuajiri jamaa na marafiki
Wananchi wana jukumu la:
Kudai uwazi katika ajira za kaunti
Kupinga ukabila na ufisadi katika kuajiri
Kuwawajibisha magavana wanaoajiri bila kuzingatia uwezo
👉 Ajira si hisani, ni haki.
4️⃣ KAUNTI ZA PWANI: MABILIONI BILA MAENDELEO
Kaunti za Pwani hupokea mabilioni ya shilingi kila mwaka kutoka serikali kuu. Lakini:
Barabara bado mbaya
Hospitali hazina dawa
Shule ziko katika hali duni
Wananchi wana jukumu la:
Kufuatilia bajeti za kaunti
Kushiriki public participation
Kuuliza: Pesa zilienda wapi?
👉 Ukiona maendeleo hakuna, pesa hazikupotea—ziliibwa.
5️⃣ UTALII NA BAHARI: RASILIMALI ZINAZONUFAISHA WACHACHE
Pwani ni kitovu cha utalii Kenya. Lakini:
Hoteli kubwa ni za wageni
Wenyeji ni walinzi na wafagiaji
Uvuvi wa kimataifa unawaacha wavuvi maskini
Wananchi wana jukumu la:
Kudai sera za kumlinda mvuvi na mfanyabiashara wa Pwani
Kuwahoji viongozi kuhusu mikataba ya bahari na utalii
Kukataa viongozi wanaonyamaza wakati rasilimali zinaporwa
👉 Bahari ni ya wananchi, si ya wawekezaji wachache.
6️⃣ KURA: SILAHA YA MWISHO YA WANANCHI
Wananchi wa Pwani wana nguvu moja kubwa: kura.
Usimchague mtu kwa sababu ni “wetu”
Usimchague mtu kwa pesa ya siku moja
Chagua kwa rekodi na matokeo
👉 Kiongozi aliyeshindwa hastahili muhula wa pili.
🔥 HITIMISHO KALI
Pwani haina tatizo la rasilimali.
Pwani haina tatizo la watu.
Pwani ina tatizo la uongozi na ukimya wa wananchi.
Mpaka wananchi wa Pwani waamue kusema HAPANA kwa uongozi mbovu,
ardhi itaendelea kuporwa,
bandari itawanufaisha wengine,
na vijana wataendelea kuhesabika kama takwimu za ukosefu wa ajira.

Klabu ya Young Africans SC (Yanga) leo Januari 13, 2025 imeandika historia nyingine baada ya kutwaa Ubingwa wa Mapinduzi Cup, taji ambalo kwa wengi huonekana dogo kwa jina, lakini kwa uhalisia wake lina uzito mkubwa ndani na nje ya uwanja.

Ushindi huu umebeba maana pana zaidi ya kombe lenyewe. Wakati Yanga ilipoamua kushusha baadhi ya wachezaji wake muhimu waliokuwa wakilitumikia Taifa kwenye mashindano ya AFCON ili kushiriki Mapinduzi Cup, kulikuwepo na mitazamo tofauti. Wapo waliodhani ni ishara ya kiu ya makombe, kana kwamba Yanga inatafuta sifa kwa gharama yoyote. Hata hivyo, mtazamo huo unapuuzia jambo la msingi: kushindwa mara kwa mara, hata kwenye mashindano madogo, kunashusha heshima ya klabu.

Katika soka la kisasa, kila mashindano ni jukwaa la kupimwa. Yanga ilichagua kupambana kwa nguvu zake zote, ikitambua kuwa Mapinduzi Cup si tu kombe la mazoezi, bali ni nembo ya heshima, ushindani na hadhi ya soka la Tanzania.
Ushindi wa Yanga unaonesha kuwa klabu za Tanzania zina uwezo wa kushindana na kushinda dhidi ya wapinzani wa kimataifa, jambo linaloimarisha taswira ya nchi yetu katika ramani ya soka Afrika.

Kwa Shirikisho la Soka Afrika (CAF), Yanga inaendelea kujijengea taswira ya klabu makini, inayoheshimu mashindano na ratiba za soka. Hii ni sifa kubwa, kwani CAF huangalia nidhamu, ushindani na hadhi ya vilabu vinavyowakilisha Afrika kwenye majukwaa ya kimataifa.

Kimataifa, ushindi kama huu huongeza brand value ya klabu. Wadhamini, waandaaji wa mashindano na wadau wa soka huanza kuiangalia Yanga kama klabu inayojali ushindi, heshima na maendeleo ya soka.

HÀNH TRÌNH TRỞ THÀNH TRIỆU PHÚ ( 14/1/2026)

Có một sự thật rất dịu dàng nhưng cũng rất tỉnh táo:
đa số chúng ta không thiếu tiền, mà thiếu một mối quan hệ đúng với tiền.

Hành trình trở thành triệu phú, nếu nhìn kỹ, thực ra gồm hai phần rất khác nhau: trở thành và triệu phú.
“Triệu phú” là kết quả mà ai cũng nhìn thấy.
Nhưng “trở thành” mới là phần quyết định, phần âm thầm, lâu dài và mang tính con người nhất.

Trước khi bạn có nhiều tiền, bạn cần trở thành một người biết quản lý tiền. Trước khi xây dựng tài sản lớn, bạn cần xây dựng kỷ luật, tư duy và kiến thức. Tiền không đến để dạy ta trưởng thành; ngược lại, chính sự trưởng thành mới giữ được tiền ở lại.

Hãy tưởng tượng tiền giống như dòng nước. Nếu không có hệ thống dẫn, nước đến đâu chảy tràn đến đó rồi biến mất. Nhưng khi bạn chia dòng nước ấy thành những “kênh” rõ ràng, mỗi kênh có mục đích riêng, thì dòng nước không chỉ được giữ lại mà còn sinh sôi. Đó chính là triết lý của việc quản lý tiền bằng các “cái lọ”. 

Có phần dành cho chi tiêu cần thiết, để cuộc sống được nhẹ nhàng.
Có phần dành cho phát triển bản thân, như học kỹ năng, mở rộng tư duy — đây là nơi gieo hạt cho tương lai.
Có phần dành cho đầu tư và tự do tài chính, để tiền dần học cách làm việc thay bạn.
Có phần tiết kiệm cho những mục tiêu lớn, tạo cảm giác an tâm.
Có phần để hưởng thụ, bởi niềm vui giúp ta không bỏ cuộc giữa đường.
Và có phần để cho đi, vì khi biết sẻ chia, ta đang nuôi dưỡng một nội tâm đủ đầy.

Ví dụ rất đời thường: hai người có cùng mức thu nhập. Một người sống theo cảm xúc, tiêu hết những gì kiếm được. Người kia đi chậm hơn, chia tiền có chủ đích, dành một phần nhỏ để học hỏi và đầu tư vào năng lực bản thân. Sau vài năm, khoảng cách giữa họ không nằm ở số tiền kiếm được — mà ở con người họ đã trở thành.

Quản lý tiền không phải để sống khắt khe. Nó giống như một phương thuốc nhẹ, chữa dần căn bệnh tài chính âm ỉ: lo lắng, bị động và thiếu lựa chọn. Khi bạn làm chủ được tiền, bạn làm chủ được nhịp sống của mình.

Và rồi, đến một lúc nào đó, “triệu phú” không còn là đích đến quá xa. Nó chỉ là hệ quả tự nhiên của một quá trình đúng.

Bởi sau cùng:trở thành triệu phú không phải là có bao nhiêu tiền trong tay, mà là trở thành người đủ bản lĩnh để tiền ở lại và sinh sôi cùng bạn!

The school's athlete deliberately tried to push me under the fountain, but I didn't panic,  I just looked at my watch—five minutes after the police chief greeted me, the whole park seemed to freeze.

Chapter 1: The Countdown
The heat in Oak Creek was the kind that stuck to you, a humid, suffocating blanket that smelled of asphalt and freshly cut grass. It was typical for late May in the suburbs, where the manicured lawns hid the rot beneath the soil, and the smiles of the neighbors never quite reached their eyes.

I sat on the edge of the stone fountain in the center of the school quad, trying to make myself as small as possible. Invisibility was a skill I had been practicing for six months. If I didn't move, if I didn't speak, if I kept my head down and my breathing shallow, sometimes the world would forget I existed.

But not today.

"Hey, Ghost."

The voice was heavy, dripping with the lazy arrogance of someone who had never been told 'no' in his entire life. Tyler Maddock.

I didn't look up. I focused on the ants marching in a line near my sneaker. They had a purpose. They had a destination. I had neither.

"I'm talking to you," Tyler said, his shadow falling over me, blocking out the sun.

I checked my watch. 12:12 PM.

Just three more minutes. If I could just survive three more minutes, the bell would ring, the chaos of the lunch period would end, and I could disappear into the library.

"Leave him alone, Ty," a girl's voice said from the periphery. Probably Jessica. She was kind, but kindness in Oak Creek was passive. It was a whisper in a hurricane.

"Shut up, Jess," Tyler snapped. He kicked the leg of my jeans. It wasn't hard enough to bruise, just hard enough to humiliate. "He thinks he's too good for us. Look at him. Doesn't even wear the school colors. Just that stupid grey hoodie every single day."

I slowly closed the book I was reading. It wasn't a textbook; it was a manual on structural engineering. Bridges. How to build things that connect one side to another. How to build things that don't collapse under pressure.

"I don't want any trouble, Tyler," I said. My voice sounded foreign to my own ears. Rusty.

"That's the problem, Liam. You're boring," Tyler laughed, looking back at his entourage—Kyle and Mason, two linebacker-sized boys who mimicked everything Tyler did, like funhouse mirror reflections of his ego. "You've been here half a year, and nobody knows a damn thing about you. Where you from? Who's your daddy? Why do you flinch when a car backfires?"

He reached down and grabbed the strap of my backpack.

My heart hammered against my ribs. Not fear—adrenaline. Trained reflex.

"Don't," I said, my hand shooting out to grab the other strap.

"Oh? The Ghost has a grip!" Tyler yanked hard. He was stronger than me. He had protein shakes and a personal trainer; I had insomnia and a diet of cafeteria apples.

He ripped the bag from my hands.

"Give it back," I said, standing up. The sudden movement made the crowd around us gasp. The Ghost never stood up.

"What's in here?" Tyler unzipped the main compartment. He started pulling things out and tossing them onto the concrete. A pen case. A calculator. A bruised apple.

Then, his hand pulled out the black leather sketchbook.

Everything in my body went cold. The world narrowed down to that black rectangle in his beefy hand.

"No," I said. It wasn't a request. It was a warning.

That book contained the only image I had left of her face before the accident. Before the trial. Before the Witness Protection Program erased my name, my history, and my soul. It was a drawing I had spent three months perfecting, trying to capture the exact way her eyes crinkled when she laughed. If I lost that, I lost her all over again.

Tyler saw the panic in my eyes. He fed on it.

"Important?" He held it over the fountain water. The green, murky water circulated by a rusty pump.

"Tyler, please," I said. "Drop anything else. Just give me the book."

"Beg," he smiled.

I looked at my watch. 12:14 PM.

I couldn't beg. I literally couldn't. The psychologists had explained it to me—trauma response. When pushed into a corner, I didn't fawn; I froze.

"I'm waiting," Tyler sang.

When I didn't speak, his smile faltered. He hated that I wouldn't give him the satisfaction. He hated that my silence felt louder than his shouting.

"Oops," he said, deadpan.

He opened his hand.

I lunged, but Mason caught me by the hood of my sweatshirt, jerking me back.

I watched in slow motion as the black leather hit the surface. It didn't float. The heavy paper, the leather binding—it drank the water immediately. It sank beneath the algae, disappearing into the dark sludge at the bottom.

A sound escaped my throat. A strangled, broken noise.

"There," Tyler dusted his hands off. "Now you have a reason to cry. Go ahead. Cry for us, Ghost."

The crowd was laughing. Dozens of phones were raised, recording the 'EPIC FAIL' of the weird kid.

I stopped struggling against Mason. I went perfectly still.

I looked at my watch.

12:15 PM.

The Protocol.

My handler, Agent Sarah Vance, had given me strictly specific instructions. 'Check-in is at 12:15 PM daily. If you do not text the code word, we assume you are compromised. If you are compromised, we assume you are dead or taken. We send the cavalry.'

I hadn't texted. My phone was in the bottom of the fountain, inside the front pocket of the backpack.

"What are you looking at?" Tyler shoved me. "Time for your nap?"

"Three minutes," I muttered.

"What?"

"You have three minutes," I said, looking Tyler in the eye. For the first time, he saw something there that wasn't teenage angst. He saw the thousand-yard stare of someone who had seen bodies in the trunks of cars. "Run."

"Are you threatening me?" Tyler laughed, looking around for validation. "Did you hear that? He threatened me!"

He raised his fist. "I think you need a lesson in respect."

"Tyler, stop!" Mr. Henderson, the history teacher, finally pushed through the crowd. He looked terrified. Not of Tyler, but of the situation. He was a weak man who hated conflict. "Break it up. Now."

"Stay out of this, Henderson," Tyler spat. "Unless you want your tires slashed again."

Mr. Henderson flinched. The faculty was afraid of the football team. The town worshipped them. They were the gods of Oak Creek.

I didn't look at the teacher. I looked at the gate.

12:16 PM.

"You're going to pay for that book," I said calmly.

"With what money? You wear the same clothes every day," Tyler mocked.

12:17 PM.

The air changed.

It started as a vibration in the ground. Then, the sound of engines. Not the polite hum of suburban SUVs, but the roar of high-performance engines pushed to the redline.

Sirens wailed. Not one. A chorus.

The laughter in the courtyard died instantly.

Three black SUVs tore through the open school gates, ignoring the speed bumps, launching into the air and slamming down with a shower of sparks. A police cruiser drifted sideways, blocking the exit.

"What the hell?" Mason let go of my hoodie.

Students screamed and scattered.

The doors of the SUVs flew open before the wheels had even stopped rolling. Men in tactical gear poured out. 'US MARSHALS' was emblazoned on their vests in yellow letters. They had rifles. They weren't pointing them at the students, but they were ready.

And from the lead police cruiser stepped Chief Miller.

He was a legend in this town. A man of absolute iron. He had been the one to arrest the Mayor two years ago. He was untouchable.

Tyler looked like he was about to vomit. "I... I didn't do anything! It was a prank! We were just—"

Chief Miller didn't even blink at him. He marched through the puddle of water, his boots splashing heavily. He pushed Tyler aside with one hand, sending the quarterback sprawling onto the wet concrete.

The Chief stopped in front of me. The courtyard was silent enough to hear the water trickling in the fountain.

I stood there, soaking wet, shivering, my hands empty.

Chief Miller looked at his watch. Then he looked at me. His face was pale. He thought he was too late. He thought the cartel had found me.

When he saw I was alive, just wet and bullied, a wave of relief washed over his hardened face.

He snapped his heels together. The sound echoed off the brick walls of the school. He raised his hand to his brow. A perfect salute.

"Asset Secure," he barked. "Falcon is safe."

The tactical team lowered their weapons slightly.

"Get in the car, son," Miller said, his voice dropping to a gentle tone the town had never heard. "We’re burning this location. Cover is blown."

I looked down at Tyler. He was on his knees, looking up at me with absolute terror. He realized then that the hierarchy of high school meant nothing in the real world. He realized that while he was playing football, I was playing a game of life and death.

"My book," I said to the Chief. "It's in the water."

Chief Miller turned to his deputy. "Retrieve it. Bag it as evidence. If it's damaged..." He turned his cold eyes to Tyler. "Charge him with destruction of Federal Property and assault on a Protected Witness."

"Federal?" Tyler squeaked.

I turned my back on him. I walked toward the open door of the armored SUV.

I left my life at Oak Creek High behind, but as I climbed into the dark leather seat, I knew one thing: I wasn't the victim anymore.

When the System Fails Women, Charlatans Move In: A Birth Worker’s Response to The Birth Keepers.

I have spent the better part of the last fifteen years teaching evidence-based childbirth education to women and their partners. For more than a decade, I have also worked as a birth doula, supporting women emotionally through pregnancy, birth, and the fragile early weeks of motherhood.

So, I listened to The Guardian’s podcast series The Birth Keepers with a mix of professional interest and mounting horror.
It is a compelling investigation. It is also deeply, deeply distressing.
The series documents the rise of the so-called “Free Birth Society” (FBS), the ideology it promotes, the women it draws in, the tragedies it leaves behind, and the business empire built in the aftermath of those tragedies.

It is a story about vulnerability, persuasion, misinformation, and the very real consequences of abandoning evidence-based care.
I want to take a position that I know will be unpopular in some corners of the birth world:

I do not support freebirth.

Let me be very clear about what that does not mean.
It does not mean I oppose physiological birth. Supporting normal, undisturbed birth is at the core of everything I teach and advocate for. It does not mean I am blind to the way pregnancy and birth - particularly in the Global North - have become increasingly medicalised, procedural, and intervention-heavy. And it certainly does not mean I deny the reality of the skyrocketing rates of birth trauma being reported by women around the world, often after experiences of disrespectful care and, in some cases, outright obstetric violence.

All of those realities are, in fact, central to this story.
They are exactly what has driven more and more women to look for alternatives to mainstream maternity care. And they are exactly what opportunists like Emilee Saldaya and Yolande Norris-Clark have seized upon - building an ideology, a following, and a business model that preys on women who are frightened, disillusioned, and desperate to avoid being harmed again by a system that has already failed them.

There is no serious debate to be had about whether the maternity system, as it currently operates in many countries, is fit for purpose.
We have known for a long time - and the research is remarkably consistent on this - that the best outcomes for mothers and babies are associated with:

• Continuity of care by a known midwife
• High-quality, trusting relationships with caregivers
• Culturally safe, trauma-informed care
• Woman-centred, respectful care where women are genuinely involved in decisions
• High-quality, independent, evidence-based childbirth education 

When women receive this kind of care, outcomes improve. Satisfaction improves. Trauma decreases. Intervention rates fall.
And crucially: the perceived need to “opt out” entirely of the system all but disappears.

This is the part that rarely gets said out loud.

I genuinely do not believe that most women would ever choose to freebirth if they had access to safe, respectful, relational, evidence-based maternity care - including access to properly supported homebirth with a qualified midwife.

I am a strong advocate for homebirth. Healthy women with low-risk pregnancies are often excellent candidates for planned homebirth with a skilled midwife. The outcomes in privately practising midwifery models speak for themselves: excellent clinical results, and extremely high maternal satisfaction.

This is not a debate between “hospital birth” and “natural birth”. It is a debate about quality, safety, respect, and relationships.
There is also a lot of lazy fearmongering in mainstream discourse about birth - the tired line that “before modern medicine women and babies died all the time” - as if the only alternatives are hyper-medicalised obstetrics or reckless abandonment of care.

The truth is more nuanced.

Most women will have healthy pregnancies and give birth to healthy babies. Good antenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal care is a large part of why this is so.

And a small but important percentage of women and babies will always need extra monitoring, escalation, and medical intervention. In those cases, obstetric care is not just justified - it is lifesaving.
What The Birth Keepers shows, in devastating detail, is what happens when ideology replaces clinical judgement, and when charismatic leaders replace accountable professionals. The story of Lorren Holliday and her baby, Journey Moon, should haunt every person who works anywhere near birth.

It also shows how, even after tragedy and public backlash, this ideology was not dismantled - it was repackaged, monetised, and exported globally.

This is not empowerment. It is exploitation.

Saldaya and Norris-Clark are not brave truth-tellers standing up to a broken system. They are selling dangerous misinformation via websites, online courses, private consultations, and closed online communities - and they should be legally accountable for the harm that flows from it.

Words matter. Advice matters. Influence matters.

And when people position themselves as authorities in an area where the margin for error is measured in lives, they must be held to account.

None of this lets the maternity system off the hook.
In fact, the most confronting message of this entire series is this:
If women are prepared to risk their own lives and their babies’ lives to avoid mainstream maternity care, the system is already in profound moral and clinical crisis.

That should be a five-alarm fire for policymakers, health services, academic institutions, and governments.

Women do not need to be rescued from birth. They need to be able to trust the people and systems that care for them.

Until we build a maternity system that is genuinely safe, respectful, relational, trauma-informed, and evidence-based - not just in policy documents but in everyday practice - the vacuum will continue to be filled by people who offer certainty, belonging, and simple answers in place of complexity, humility, and real care.

And the cost of that, as this series shows, can be unbearably high.

Daddy Lumba estate battle deepens as Akosua Serwaah heads to Court of Appeal

Akosua Serwaah has filed an appeal at the Court of Appeal in Kumasi against a High Court decision that recognised both her and Priscilla Ofori, also known as Odo Broni, as the lawful surviving spouses of the late highlife legend Charles Kwadwo Fosu, popularly known as Daddy Lumba.

In a notice of appeal, Ms Serwaah is challenging the entire judgment of the Kumasi High Court, contending that the trial court erred in rejecting and declaring inadmissible a marriage certificate she tendered in support of her claim.

She further argues that the High Court committed an error of law when it held that she had failed to satisfy the requirements of the Evidence Act, 1975 (NRCD 323) for the admission of the marriage certificate into evidence.

The appellant is therefore asking the Court of Appeal to set aside the High Court’s judgment and to declare her as the sole lawful surviving spouse of the late musician.

On November 28, 2025, the Kumasi High Court, presided over by Justice Dr Dorinda Smith Arthur, dismissed Ms Serwaah’s suit, in which she sought a declaration that she was the only surviving spouse of Daddy Lumba.

The court held that the plaintiff failed to establish that she was married to the deceased under the Marriage Ordinance in a manner that would make her the sole surviving spouse.

According to the court, the evidence on record showed that Daddy Lumba married Akosua Serwaah under customary law, which is potentially polygamous. As a result, the court found that his subsequent marriage to Odo Broni was also valid under Ghanaian law.

In conclusion, the High Court declared both Akosua Serwaah and Priscilla Ofori, alias Odo Broni, as the legally recognised surviving spouses of the late music icon.

During his early years in South Africa (1893-1914), Mahatma Gandhi made several controversial and racially insensitive statements and held views that considered Black Africans to be inferior to both white people and Indians. 
Key Statements and Actions
Derogatory Language: Gandhi frequently used the highly offensive term "kaffir" to refer to Black Africans in his writings and speeches. The word, derived from Arabic for "infidel," was a deeply derogatory racial slur.
Perception of Black Africans: He described Black Africans as "savage, raw, and living a life of indolence and nakedness".
Demands for Segregation: One of his early legal battles involved campaigning for Indians to have separate post office entrances from Black people, explicitly to avoid being "classed with the natives of South Africa". He also expressed strong objection to Indians and Black Africans mixing in prisons or social life.
Racial Hierarchy: In a 1903 letter, he wrote that white people in South Africa should be the "predominating race" and argued that white people and Indians were part of an "Aryan brotherhood" and superior to Africans on a "civilised scale".
Political Stance: Gandhi focused primarily on the rights of the Indian community, often aligning himself with British colonizers and not making common cause with African liberation struggles during his early years. He even served in the British Indian Ambulance Corps during the Anglo-Boer War and the Bambatha Rebellion.

Moody Awori was born in 1927 in Butere though his parents Canon Jeremiah Awori and Mariamu Awori came from Funyula, Busia county.

Moody Awori or Uncle Moody popularly known in Kenya first became a MP of Funyula in 1983 using KANU as the political party then under Daniel Moi.

Moody Awori became the 9th Vice President of Kenya when Michael Kijana Wamalwa died in 2003. He was the VP from 25th September 2003 to 9th January 2008 where Kalonzo Musyoka was picked Mwai Kibaki as the 10th VP president of Kenya.

Of course in the 2007 general elections, Moody Awori had lost his MP position to Paul Otuoma 

Since his last active participation in office as VP and MP, the 98 year old has led a quiet life.

In fact he was not involved in abusive politics like most politicians do.

This may explain the reason behind his long life. No politician according to my knowledge has lived longer like Uncle Moody.

He's my role model to this regard. Quiet life after retirement. Minding his own business.

     Long live Uncle Moody Awori  🙏.

Nyota hii inatawala mabega, mikono, viganja na sehemu ya juu ya mbavu.Tatizo la kutopumzika kwa sababu ya kutafuta mambo mapya ndio yanayosababisha maradhi kwa wenye nyota hii.Wanasahau miili yao na mara nyingi wanapata matatizo ya neva kutokana na uchovu kwa mishughuliko mingi.Magonjwa yao makubwa ni kukosa pumzi (bronchitis), pumu (asthma), matatizo ya kifua, mafua, flu, ajali za mara kwa mara kwenye mikono na mabega.

Mapacha wanashauriwa wapende kula vyakula vifuatavyo ambavyo ndio vinavyotawaliwa na nyota yao, kuku, rasiberi, karoti na uduvi.

Are You Going Through a Dry Spell?
~David Wilkerson 

Have you ever sat in church and watched those all around you getting blessed while you feel nothing? They cry; they pray; they worship with tremendous feelings. But you are not moved upon at all. You begin to wonder if there is something wrong with your spiritual life. 

I believe all true believers experience dry spells at various times in their Christian lives. Even Jesus felt the isolation when he cried aloud, “Father, why have you forsaken me?”

Without the nearness of God, there can be no peace. The dryness can be stopped only with the dew of his glory. The despair can be dispelled only by the assurance that God is answering. The fire of the Holy Ghost must heat the mind, body and soul.

Come to the water that satisfies that soul thirst. Come to the Father who pities his children. Come to the Lord of life who promises to forgive every sin committed. Come to the one who refuses to condemn you or forsake you or hide from you.

Nothing dispels dryness and emptiness more quickly than an hour or two shut in with God. Putting off that date with God in his secret closet causes guilt. We know our love for him should lead us into his presence, but we busy ourselves in so many other things; then time slips away, and God is left out. We throw in his direction a whole array of “thought prayers.” But nothing can take the place of that secret closet with the door shut, praying to the Father in that seclusion. That is the solution to every dry spell.

God sets before you a choice. His love demands a choice. If God supernaturally lifted us out of every battle without pain or suffering, it would abort all trials and all temptation; there would be no free choice and no testing as by fire. It would be God superimposing his will on mankind. He chooses to meet us in our dryness and show us how it can become the way into a new life of faith.

It is often according to the will of God that we suffer dryness and even pain. “Wherefore let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator” (1 Pet. 4:19).

Thank God, suffering is always the short period before final victory!

Ujumbe wa Jamhuri ya Kidemokrasia ya Kongo (DRC) ukiongozwa na Waziri wa Nchi, anayeshughulikia masuala ya Ustawi wa Jamii, Hatua za Kibinadamu na Mshikamano, Eve Masudi umetembelea kambi ya Wakimbizi ya Nyarugusu mkoani Kigoma.

Masudi ametembelea ili kujionea maisha ya Wakimbizi wa DRC katika kambi hiyo na kusikiliza maombi na mapendekezo yao kwa Serikali ya DRC.

Akizungumza na Wakimbizi katika uwanja wa mikutano kambini hapo, ameishukuru Serikali ya Tanzania kwa kuendelea kutoa hifadhi Wakimbizi kutoka nchini DRC katika hali ya utu na amani kwa takribani miaka 30 tangu kuanzishwa kwa kambi hiyo. Aidha, amewaeleza kuwa Serikali ya DRC inaendelea na jitihada za kutafuta suluhisho la kuleta amani ya kudumu ili waweze kurejea nchini kwao. Pia amewasihi kuishi kwa nidhamu na maadili  ili kuilinda heshima ya DRC na kuthamini ukarimu wa Serikali ya Tanzania.

Masudi amewataka Wakimbizi walio tayari kurejea nyumbani kuendelea kujiandikisha rasmi ili waweze kurejea kwenye makazi yao na kufanya shughuli za maendeleo, mambo ambayo hawawezi kufanya wakiwa kambini.

Naye, Naibu Waziri wa Mambo ya Nje na Ushirikiano wa Afrika Mashariki, anayeshughulikia masuala ya Afrika Mashariki, James Millya amewaeleza wakimbizi hao kuwa Serikali ya Tanzania itaendelea kusimamia misingi ya Sheria za Kimataifa za uhifadhi wa Wakimbizi  hivyo, itaendelea kushirikiana nao katika kipindi chote wawapo nchini pamoja na kuwahakikishia usalama wao katika mchakato mzima wa kurejea nchini kwao. Aidha, ameeleza kuwa zoezi la kurejea nyumbani ni la hiari na si shuruti.

Akiwasilisha taarifa ya kambi, Kaimu Mkuu wa Kambi ya Nyarugusu, Samwel Kuyi ameeleza kuwa kambi ina jumla ya wakimbizi 132,404. Wakimbizi 86,918 ni kutoka DRC, 45,346 ni Warundi na 98 kutoka mataifa mengine. Zaidi ya 60% ya wakimbizi wa DRC ni watoto chini ya miaka 18 kati yao 21,660 ni watoto chini ya miaka mitano.

Moja ya wakimbizi, Apolina Masumbuko amesema wako tayari kurejea nyumbani na kuomba Serikali ya DRC iweze kurejesha amani nchini kwao ili warudi katika mazingira salama na tulivu.

The police officer stood on the front porch, notebook in hand, looking uneasy. “Sir, are you sure she didn’t just… go on vacation?”

My son, Michael, wiped sweat from his forehead. He was wearing his expensive suit, pacing the driveway of the house I had lived in for forty years. “Officer, my mother is seventy-four. She doesn’t ‘go on vacation’ without telling me. The furniture is gone. The house is empty. She’s been kidnapped, or she’s had a mental break and wandered off. You need to ping her phone!”

That’s when I pulled up in an Uber.

Not a sedan. A bright yellow Jeep with the top down.

I stepped out—well, eased out carefully, let’s not get carried away—wearing oversized sunglasses and a denim jacket I hadn’t worn since 1985.

“I haven’t been kidnapped, Michael,” I said, tipping the driver five dollars. “I moved.”

My name is Eleanor. And three months ago, I realized I was already dead—I just hadn’t stopped breathing yet.

I lived in a four-bedroom colonial in a wealthy Connecticut suburb. It was the “American Dream.” My husband, Robert, worked himself into an early grave to pay for it. After he died five years ago, that dream became a prison.

I spent my days dusting rooms no one entered. I paid a landscaping crew a small fortune to cut grass no one walked on. I paid property taxes that could have fed a small village.

Michael is a good son. He’s a hedge fund manager in Manhattan. He checks boxes.

Mom is alive? Check.
Mom has groceries? Check.
Mom is safe in the big empty box? Check.

But he didn’t see me. He saw an obligation. A fragile antique that needed to be preserved on a shelf.

The turning point wasn’t dramatic. I didn’t fall. I didn’t get sick.

I was watching the news. The anchor spoke about the “loneliness epidemic” affecting seniors and, moments later, the “housing crisis” crushing young people.

I looked around my 3,000-square-foot house—just me and the ghosts. Then I looked at my bank account, draining steadily to heat empty air.

I thought: This is stupid.

I didn’t call Michael. He would have sent a nurse or moved me to “Sunset Pines Assisted Living,” where the highlight of the day is soft-food Tuesday.

I sold the house to a developer for cash. I sold the mahogany dining table. I sold the china.

I packed two suitcases and Robert’s old toolbox.

I moved to Austin, Texas.

I didn’t move into a condo. I answered an ad for an “Intergenerational Co-Op,” a retrofitted warehouse downtown.

“We need wisdom,” the ad said. “We offer chaos and community.”

“You’re living in a commune?” Michael shouted, his face reddening as we stood on the sidewalk outside the building.

“It’s a co-op, Michael. And I’m not just living here. I’m the house manager.”

I led him inside.

The space felt alive. It smelled of coffee, soldering irons, and sourdough starter.

My roommates are the people society calls “struggling millennials” or “lazy Gen Z.” They aren’t lazy. They’re exhausted.

There’s Leo, 28, a graphic designer juggling three gigs who still can’t afford a studio. Sarah, 32, an ER nurse who saves lives all day and cries in her car over student loans. Marcus, 24, a coder who stares at screens for fourteen hours and forgets to eat.

When I first arrived, they were nervous around me. They treated me like a liability. “Eleanor, the stairs are steep.” “Eleanor, we’re playing loud music—is that okay?”

I let them fuss for about three days.

Then the Wi-Fi router mounted on a ceiling beam malfunctioned. Leo dragged over a ladder in a panic. Sarah tried calling a technician who wanted $200.

I walked over, climbed the ladder—slowly, three points of contact, thank you very much—pulled out Robert’s screwdriver, and reset the hard-line connection.

I looked down at their stunned faces. “I was fixing circuit boards for General Electric in the seventies,” I said. “Now, who’s making tea?”

Everything changed.

They didn’t need my money. They needed a mother. Not someone to judge them for not owning a home, but someone steady.

They needed someone to say, “Put the phone down. The email can wait.” Someone to show them how to sew on a button instead of buying a new shirt. Someone to call everyone to the table at seven and say, “Dinner’s ready. Sit. Talk.”

In the suburbs, I was invisible. Here, I’m essential.

When Marcus was laid off last month, he didn’t isolate himself. He sat on my bed while I told him about being fired in 1988. We drank hot cocoa, and I helped him rewrite his résumé.

When Sarah came home shattered after losing a patient, I didn’t offer platitudes. I held her hand and let her cry until she fell asleep.

And in return, they gave me my life back.

They taught me how to use a tablet. I now run a TikTok account called Ask Eleanor, where I answer questions about cooking, sewing, and heartbreak.

I have 200,000 followers.

Apparently, the world is hungry for a grandma.

Michael sat on a mismatched velvet sofa while Leo handed him a craft beer.

“I don’t get it, Mom,” Michael said, looking around at the exposed brick and laughter from the kitchen. “You had a mansion. You had peace and quiet.”

“I had silence, Michael. There’s a difference.”

I sat beside him. “In that house, I was waiting to die. I was protecting assets for you. But I’m not finished living.”

I pointed toward the kitchen, where Marcus chopped vegetables and Sarah laughed at one of Leo’s jokes.

“They’ll never own a big colonial like I did. The world has changed. It’s harder for them. They’re lonely too. We’ve got big empty houses filled with old people and small apartments filled with lonely young ones. We’re doing it wrong.”

Michael really looked at me then. He saw the denim jacket. The spark in my eyes that had been gone since his father died.

“Are you… happy?” he asked.

“I’m useful,” I said. “And I’m loved. And tonight we’re making tacos. You should stay.”

He loosened his tie and took a sip of beer. “I do like tacos.”

I see so many people my age complaining online that the younger generation is “soft” or “entitled.”

They’re not. They’re fighting battles we never had to face, in an economy that doesn’t love them back.

And us? We’re sitting in paid-off fortresses, dying of isolation.

The American Dream used to be a picket fence. I think the new American Dream is a long dinner table.

Don’t wait for your kids to call. Don’t wait for silence to swallow you. Sell the house. Buy the ticket. Share what you know.

My name is Eleanor. I’m seventy-four years old. And for the first time in years, I can’t wait for tomorrow morning.

Ndani yao, kuna sauti ndogo isiyopiga kelele, lakini haichoki kunong’ona:
“Hapa sio mahali pangu.”
Lakini badala ya kuisikiliza, wanavaa tabasamu kama barakoa, ili maswali yasiwe mengi Wanabaki kwenye kazi zilizokufa, mahusiano yaliyooza, na ndoto zisizopumua tena, kwa sababu kuondoka kunahitaji ujasiri mkubwa kuliko kubaki.

Paulo Coelho aliwahi kuandika katika The Alchemist:
“Watu wengi huishi maisha ya mtu mwingine, sio yao.”
Na ndipo huzuni ya kizazi chetu inapoanzia  kuishi ndoto za watu wengine huku tukizika sauti zetu.

Cha kusikitisha zaidi: roho haidanganyiki.

Maya Angelou alisema:
“Hakuna uchungu mkubwa kuliko kubeba ndani yako maisha ambayo hukuwahi kuyaishi.”

Subira huzaa matunda, lakini kuishi maisha yasiyo yako hukunyima furaha, hukupokonya nguvu, na mwisho hukufanya uwe kivuli cha mtu uliyepaswa kuwa.
Sikiliza, kizazi cha sasa.

“Maisha yako ni mafupi sana acha  kuishi ndoto za mtu mwingine.”

Sio kila kitu kilichopo kwenye maisha yako kinastahili kubaki.
Sio kila mtu anayekuzunguka ana tiketi ya kukaa milele.
Wengine walikuja kama somo, sio hatima. Wengine walitumwa kukuonyesha wewe ni nani, kisha waondoke.

Kutoka Afrika, Nelson Mandela alituachia maneno mazito kama upepo wa uhuru:
“Uhuru wa kweli ni kuishi maisha yanayoheshimu utu wako.”

Na hakuna heshima ya utu katika kuishi mahali ambapo roho yako inazimwa kila siku.
Na siku utakapoamua kujichagua, itauma mwanzoni.

unarudi nyumbani kwako mwenyewe. Unaanza kupumua tena. Unasikia sauti yako halisi, ile uliyokuwa umeifunga kwa muda mrefu.

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie alisema:
“Ukikaa kimya ili ukubalike, unajifuta mwenyewe.”
Usijifute. Jiandike upya.
Maisha hayakuumbwa yaishiwe kwa hofu.
Uliumbwa uishi mahali ambapo moyo wako unapanuka, sio unapojifinya.

Na kama ndani yako kuna sauti inayosema, “Hapa sio pangu,” hiyo sio udhaifu  hiyo ni hekima ya roho yako ikikuita urudi kwenye ukweli wako.

Ndipo utaanza kuishi kweli, sio kuigiza kuishi.

Pongal is a Hindu festival which is observed by people of Tamil Nadu. Pongal is a four-day festival, and the most important day of Pongal is known as Thai Pongal. Thai Pongal which is the second day of the four day festivity is also celebrated as Sankranti. The same day is observed as Makar Sankranti in North Indian states when people take a holy dip in river Ganges.

The day before Thai Pongal is known as Bogi Pandigai. On this day people clean their homes and light a bonfire to discard unused items. 

In Punjab the same day is celebrated as Lohri by the Sikh community.

Pongal / Makar Sankranti is celebrated by boiling freshly harvested rice with fresh milk and jaggery in a new clay pot. While boiling the concoction, people let the milk spill over the pot as an auspicious sign of material abundance and prosperity. Later the concoction of rice, milk and jaggery, known as Pongal, is topped with brown sugar, Ghee, cashew nuts and raisins. Freshly cooked Pongal is first offered to the Sun God as a gratitude for good harvesting and later served on banana leaves to the people present in the home for the ceremony. Traditionally Pongal is cooked at sunrise at an open place.

Veneration of sacred cows and family gatherings are also done.

Inimesed suhtuvad oma hirmudesse suhteliselt alistuvalt  - on nagu on, las ta siis olla. Kuid lihtsad ja levinud hirmud peidavad enda taha hoopis midagi, mis toimub inimese alateadvuses ja kui ta sealt välja tirida ja päikese kätte asetada, on võimalik ta ka vabaks lasta. 

Eesti maod on suhteliselt süütud ja pisikesed võrreldes oma liigikaaslastega soojades maades. Hoolimata sellest kardavad mõned eestlased ka neid tegelasi. Kuid alateadvuses on madu seotud erinevate omadustega. Neid peetakse nii väga tarkadeks kui ka salakavalateks. Oleneb millise nurga alt vaadata. Inimene, kes kardab madusid, kardab tegelikult, et teised inimesed võivad tema selja taga olla pahatahtlikud ja mürgised. Madude kartjad on ka ise tihtipeale silmakirjalikud ja tunnevad teiste vastu kadedust ja vajadust kätte maksta. Madu on ka uuestisünni sümbol, kuna vahetab nahka. Hirm madude ees võib tähendada ka hirmu, et on vaja teha suur sisemine muutus, et saada paremaks inimeseks. 

Ämblik seondub tavaliselt tema võrkudega, kuigi on ka ämblikke, kes saaki võrguga ei püüa. Eesti keeles on olemas sõna "võrgutama", mis annab edasi ämblikuhirmu sügavama sisu. Üldiselt tegelevad võrgutamisega naised ja ämblik sümboliseeribki omandihimulist ja kontrollivat naisenergiat. Inimesed, kes kardavad ämblikke, kardavad sügaval sisemuses, et keegi võib nendega manipuleerida ja sellega oma võrkudesse mähkida. Tavaliselt on inimestel, kes kardavad ämblikke, kehv suhe oma emaga, kuna nad alateadlikult kardavad teda. Kehv suhe emaga tähendab ka kehva suhet oma sisemise naiseliku poolega. Kuna neil on hirm kaotada oma vabadus sügaval sees, siis nad õpivad ka ise manipuleerimise ja võrgutamise ära, mis teeb neid veelgi rohkem naiselike salaplaanide ees jõuetuks.

WHO YAONYA KUWA VINYWAJI VYA BEI RAHISI VINAONGEZA MAGONJWA YANAYOZUILIKA.

Katika ripoti mbili mpya za kimataifa, WHO imesema ushuru mdogo na usiopangwa ipasavyo unaacha bidhaa zinazodhuru afya ziendelee kuwa rahisi kununua, wakati nchi nyingi zikikabiliwa na mifumo ya afya iliyoelemewa na mzigo wa magonjwa yasiyoambukiza NCDs na majeraha yanayozuilika.

“Kodi ya afya ni miongoni mwa nyenzo zenye nguvu zaidi tulizo nazo za kulinda afya na kuzuia magonjwa,” amesema Dkt. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Mkurugenzi Mkuu wa WHO. 

Ameongeza kuwa “Kwa kuongeza kodi kwenye bidhaa kama tumbaku, vinywaji vyenye sukari na pombe, serikali zinaweza kupunguza matumizi hatarishi na kufungua rasilimali za kifedha kwa huduma muhimu za afya.”

Katika ripoti hizo WHO imebainisha kuwa soko la kimataifa la vinywaji vyenye sukari na vileo huzalisha faida ya mabilioni ya dola kila mwaka. 
Hata hivyo, serikali hunufaika kwa kiwango kidogo tu kupitia kodi unaolenga afya, huku jamii zikibeba gharama za muda mrefu za kiafya na kiuchumi.

Kwa mujibu wa shirika hilo, mifumo dhaifu ya ushuru imeshindwa kuendana na mfumuko wa bei na ongezeko la kipato, jambo linalofanya pombe na vinywaji vyenye sukari kuwa nafuu zaidi kadri muda unavyopita katika nchi nyingi mwelekeo unaohusishwa moja kwa moja na matumizi makubwa na mzigo mkubwa wa magonjwa.

Ripoti zinaonyesha kuwa angalau nchi 116 hutoza ushuru kwa vinywaji vyenye sukari, hasa soda. 

Hata hivyo, bidhaa nyingi zenye sukari nyingi bado hazitozwi kodi, zikiwemo juisi za matunda asilimia 100, vinywaji vya maziwa vilivyoongezwa sukari, na kahawa au chai zilizo tayari kunywa.

Ingawa asilimia 97 ya nchi hutoza ushuru kwa vinywaji vya kuongeza nguvu, WHO inasema kiwango hiki hakijabadilika tangu mwaka 2023, ikionyesha kusimama kwa maendeleo. 

Kwa wastani, kodi ya vinywaji vyenye sukari inachangia takriban asilimia 2 tu ya bei ya rejareja ya soda ya kawaida kiwango kilicho chini sana kuathiri matumizi.

Ripoti tofauti ya WHO imebaini kuwa nchi 167 hutoza ushuru wa aina fulani kwa vileo, huku nchi 12 zikikataza pombe kabisa. 

Pamoja na hilo, pombe imekuwa nafuu zaidi, au bei kubaki bila kubadilika, katika nchi nyingi tangu mwaka 2022.

Mvinyo hauwekewi ushuru katika takriban nchi 25, nyingi zikiwa Ulaya, licha ya kile WHO ilichoeleza kuwa “hatari za kiafya zilizo wazi na zilizothibitishwa.”

Kwa mujibu wa Dkt. Etienne Krug, Mkurugenzi wa Idara ya WHO ya Vigezo vya Afya, Uhamasishaji na Kinga “Pombe inapokuwa nafuu zaidi, huongeza vurugu, majeraha na magonjwa. Wakati sekta inanufaika, umma hubeba madhara ya kiafya na jamii hulipa gharama za kiuchumi.”

Kwa kiwango cha kimataifa, WHO imegundua kuwa wastani wa sehemu ya ushuru wa forodha bado ni mdogo, ukiwa karibu asilimia 14 ya bei ya bia na asilimia 22.5 kwa vinywaji vikali.

WHO imesisitiza kuwa ushuru dhaifu unaendelea kuwepo licha ya uungwaji mkono mkubwa wa umma. 

Utafiti wa Gallup wa mwaka 2022 ulionesha kuwa watu wengi walioulizwa waliunga mkono kuongeza kodi kwa pombe na vinywaji vyenye sukari.

Shirika hilo linazitaka serikali kuongeza na kubuni upya kodi ya afya chini ya mpango wake mpya wa “3 kwa 35”, unaolenga kuongeza bei halisi za tumbaku, pombe na vinywaji vyenye sukari ifikapo mwaka 2035.

WHO imesema “Kuendelea kufanya bidhaa hizi kuwa ghali zaidi kwa muda si tu sera bora ya kifedha bali ni uwekezaji muhimu katika kulinda afya ya watu na kuokoa maisha.”

Life Is Not Merely Material
Md. Zahid Hossain  
Short Story | January 14, 2026  

Life does not run on material things alone.  

Money, houses, cars—they grant only passing happiness. But the real value of life is determined by our feelings, by love, and by the relationships we nurture.  

A single smile, a soft word,  
a gentle touch—these small things are what truly make our life complete.  

Material Pleasure vs. Inner Peace

We spend so much time chasing riches, believing that things will bring us joy. But is that really enough?  

If there is no peace within wealth itself, it can never fulfill the deeper quality of life.  
A beautiful moment, the warmth of sincere love, a relationship built on honesty—these bring enduring happiness.  

The Importance of Relationships and Emotions

Much of human happiness comes from our connections with others.  
Time spent with a friend, with family, or with someone beloved—where feelings matter more than words.  

We discover joy in the tiniest moments:  
stories shared over a cup of tea,  
eyes meeting in quiet understanding,  
the simple sound of someone’s laughter.  

The more we truly feel, the more we value the people around us, the more that joy becomes our real treasure.  

Love and Joy

The greatest gift life can offer is love.  
Love is not just about giving or receiving;  
it is something to be deeply experienced.  
A wordless smile, a hand brushing lightly against another,  
a quiet message sent with care—these are the true roots of life’s joy.  

No possession can ever produce such feelings.  
Greater wealth does not mean greater happiness.  
Authentic happiness flows from the stillness of the heart.  

Inner Peace and a Clearer View of Life

We can never measure life purely by material standards.  
The depth of joy we feel,  
the amount of love we share—  
this is what truly gives life its worth.  

A person’s smile, time spent laughing with friends,  
a moment of silent understanding—  
these are the genuine riches of existence.  

Personal Reflection

I have run after things many times in my life.  
Yet I have come to understand:  
whatever is truly important  
cannot be purchased—it can only be felt deep within.  

No matter how much money we earn,  
no matter how many objects we gather,  
if our heart remains empty of feeling,  
then life becomes motionless.  

Therefore—life truly consists of relationships, love, emotions, and those small, precious joys.  
These are the very foundation of our happiness and inner harmony.  

Life is not merely material.
A life filled with love, feeling, connection, and quiet delight—that is the real wealth.  

Savour every moment.  
Cherish each smile, each gesture of love, each tiny spark of joy.  
Because these feelings are the true meaning of life.  

Have you ever really understood  
that life’s deepest happiness is not found in things,  
but hidden quietly within emotions and love?

To the soccer moms in their white SUVs idling in the pickup line, I looked like a threat. They locked their doors when I walked by. I was used to it.

But my hands were shaking.

In my left hand, I held a small box wrapped in holographic unicorn paper. Inside was a silver locket with a picture of us from five years ago. Before the divorce. Before the stint in state prison for aggravated assault—a bar fight that went too far when someone touched my wife. Before I became a ghost in my own daughter’s life.

It was Lily’s eighth birthday.

“Just drop it off at the office, Jackson,” I muttered to myself, repeating the agreement I’d made with my ex-wife, Sarah. “Don’t cause a scene. Don’t scare her. Be a ghost.”

I walked toward the brick building, the smell of fresh-cut grass and playground mulch hitting me. It smelled like innocence. It smelled like a world I didn’t belong in.

I checked in at the front desk. The secretary, a woman with glasses on a chain named Mrs. Gable, looked at the “Hellrazors MC” patch on my chest and swallowed hard. Her fingers hovered over the phone.

“I’m just here to drop this off for Lily Miller,” I said, my voice gravelly. I tried to smile, to look like a dad and not a felon, but I think it just looked like a grimace. “Room 302?”

“I… I can take that for you, sir,” she stammered, her eyes darting to the security guard down the hall.

“Please,” I said, softer this time. “I just want to peek in the window. Just want to see her. I won’t go in. I promise. Five seconds.”

Maybe she saw the desperation in my eyes. Maybe she just wanted the biker out of her office before parents started complaining. She nodded nervously. “Down the hall. Third door on the left. Please be quick.”

I walked down the hallway. It was polished linoleum and crayon drawings taped to the walls. My heavy boots squeaked, echoing too loud in the quiet corridor. I felt like a bull in a china shop, terrified I’d break the silence just by breathing.

I reached Room 302.

I didn’t stand in front of the glass. I stood to the side, leaning in just enough to see through the wire-mesh window.

The class was in the middle of something. Math, maybe. Or reading.

Then I saw her.

Lily. She was sitting in the second row. She looked so much like her mother—blonde curls, delicate features—but she had my chin. She was wearing a yellow dress—her favorite color.

But she wasn’t smiling. She was shrinking.

A man was standing over her desk. Mr. Sterling. I knew the name from the emails Sarah forwarded me. He was tall, thin, wearing a cheap gray suit that looked two sizes too big. He was red in the face, veins bulging in his neck. He was shouting.

I couldn’t hear the words through the thick fire door, but I saw the body language. It’s the universal language of bullies. He slammed a book down on her desk.

Lily flinched. Her shoulders touched her ears.

My grip tightened on the unicorn box. The cardboard crinkled in my fist.

Walk away, Jackson. You’re not supposed to be here. If you go in there, you go back to jail.

But I couldn’t move. My boots were nailed to the floor.

Lily looked up at him, her mouth moving. She was saying something. Explaining? Apologizing?

Mr. Sterling didn’t like it. He leaned down, getting right in her face. He was bullying her. A grown man, intimidating an eight-year-old girl because he had a bad day. The other kids were laughing. Some were pointing.

Lily put her face in her hands.

Then, it happened.

It happened in slow motion, but also faster than a heartbeat.

Lily pushed her chair back, trying to stand up, trying to get away from his yelling.

Mr. Sterling reached out. He didn’t grab her shoulder to sit her down.

He swung his open hand.

CRACK.

Even through the heavy door, I felt the vibration of it.

He slapped her. Hard. Right across her left cheek.

Lily’s head snapped to the side. She stumbled and fell against the desk next to her.

Silence.

I watched her hand go to her face. I watched the shock register in her eyes. I watched the tears start to well up—not from sadness, but from pure, stinging pain.

The world went red.

The promise to Sarah dissolved. The probation terms dissolved. The fear of going back to prison dissolved.

The only thing that existed was the image of that man’s hand on my daughter’s face.

I didn’t turn the knob. I didn’t knock.

I stepped back, lifted my size-thirteen boot, and kicked the door right below the lock.

BOOM.

The wood splintered with a sound like a gunshot. The door swung inward so hard it smashed against the interior wall, cracking the plaster.

Every head in the room whipped toward me.

Mr. Sterling spun around, his hand still tingling, his eyes widening as he saw the frame of the door filled with black leather and pure violence.

I stepped into the room. The air felt electric.

“You…” I breathed out, the word vibrating in my chest like a growl.

I dropped the unicorn box on the floor.

“You made a mistake,” I said, my voice barely a whisper, but it carried to the back of the room. “A fatal mistake.”

Mr. Sterling took a step back, bumping into the chalkboard. “Who… who are you? You can’t be in here!”

I cracked my knuckles.

"I'm the consequences."

Be Content With What You Have

Ngozi was a hardworking woman, a tailor known for her neat hand and honest work. Her small shop sat beside a big boutique owned by her friend, Amaka. Every day, Ngozi watched customers troop into Amaka’s boutique — cars parked outside, music playing, people laughing and shopping freely.
Though Ngozi’s work put food on her table and sent her children to school, she began to feel unhappy. “God, when will my own life shine?” she often whispered.
One day, Amaka told her about a “quick investment” that promised double returns in a week. Ngozi, tired of her slow progress, borrowed money meant for her daughter’s school fees and joined in. The first week, it worked — she got double. Excited, she sold her sewing machine and invested all her savings the next time.
That was the beginning of her downfall. The scheme crashed, the organizers vanished, and Ngozi was left with nothing — no machine, no savings, no peace. Her children stayed home from school, and she had to start from scratch again.
Months later, Amaka’s boutique also closed down — her wealth was built on credit and debt. Meanwhile, Ngozi slowly rebuilt her shop, this time wiser and humbler.
One afternoon, while sewing under the shade of a mango tree, Ngozi smiled and said to herself,
“Peace in small things is better than sorrow in plenty.”
Moral:
Discontent leads to destruction. Learn to appreciate what you have, work patiently, and grow steadily — because true wealth is peace, not possession.

A Little Boy Pointed at the Police Officer’s Tattoo and Said, “My Dad Had the Same One”—It Was a Quiet Morning Patrol, Until the Officer Froze in Place. “He Pointed at My Tattoo and Said, ‘My Dad Had the Same One,’—I Was Just Doing My Morning Patrol, But That One Sentence Split My Life in Two,” because that quiet morning, with no sirens and no calls, was supposed to be routine until a small boy stopped me on the sidewalk and stared at my arm like he’d found something familiar. I laughed it off at first, then realized the symbol he pointed to wasn’t common, and that only one other person in the world shared it with me. As the boy spoke, pieces began to fall into place—his father’s eyes, his height, the way his memory slowly slipped away—and suddenly the past I had buried came rushing back. He lived in a state home, he said, waiting for parents who never came, and the woman in charge went pale when I mentioned my brother’s name, like she had been holding that truth in her chest for years. I learned the boy had been found alone, calling for a man who vanished after an accident, and that his mother still called once a month, always promising to return. Guilt crept in as I realized pride and silence had kept me from knowing my own nephew existed. I searched hospitals, records, back roads, until I finally stood face to face with a man who looked like me but no longer remembered who he was. When I told him he had a son, his hands shook, because he had been dreaming of that child without knowing why. We came back together, unsure and afraid, and when the boy saw him, he didn’t ask questions—he simply knew. He hugged us both, like we had never been apart, and for a moment everything felt whole again. Heyyyyyyy Friendsssss 🤍☀️✨

So one of the questions I get the most is, “Girl what kind of diet are you on?” And my answer is always “I eat what I want” , but how am I able to and still drop the weight/fat? 

Well first let me get transparent with you, I had eating issues, I would starve all day (no purposely, just didn’t get hungry) and then binge at night or on the worse cases not eat at all, and then gorge an entire day. I know exactly how I got to 250lbs and I had to be honest with myself. So I started with making sure I ate at least 3 meals a day, which is harder than you think. I lost my first 10lbs before i even stepped foot in the gym. 

Once my body adjusted to that and it became “normal”, I got my body used to the gym before I started counting calories, macros, and logging everything. One of yall actually told me about the app fatsecret, which I fell in love with (I stopped tracking 3 months in), it was so easy to use and calculated all my daily intakes! 

I’m a numbers girl, so as I researched and learned about calorie deficits, intakes, macros, etc, and it became so fun to start reading labels and finding low calorie, GREAT TASTING, healthier options. I knew I’d quit if I started cutting things out and limiting myself, so imagine how excited I was when the light bulb popped that I didn’t have to do that! 

So what I have below is the fatsecret app that I used and all of the substitutions and snacks I found that replaced my higher calorie ones. I also prioritized protein, which helped to hit my goals as well. Everything below I have used myself, my kids also eat them, which if you know Kason, he’s PICKY. I still eat pasta, bread, soda, and snacky foods. Literally still eat an apple fritter or ice cream every night before bed still 🤣 I say all this to say, you don’t have to restrict yourself, just need to make a few changes in your everyday foods. 

So save these, read this, do whatever, all I ask is you share or tag a friend that may need to see this too! Let’s helps spread the knowledge. I wanna see everyone feel good about themselves! 🤍💪🏽

The milk cake was soft and fluffy with perfectly balanced sweetness. A really nice, comforting dessert after all that spicy food.

Rocky was found in Arusha with an alarmingly swollen belly. This kind of condition can be caused by a heavy worm infestation or by liver disease. The person who found him brought him straight to our clinic and told us he would take Rocky home once his treatment was finished, though when that might be is still uncertain. 😔

At first, Rocky’s large, fluid-filled belly improved significantly after deworming, and we truly believed he would be ready to go home soon. But then his condition suddenly changed. He stopped eating, became very weak, and needed fluid therapy. Our clinic team ran all the tests possible within the scope of our facilities. 🏨

Eventually, we concluded that Rocky is likely suffering from liver disease. With medication, he improved once again, only to decline again just when we thought he was stable enough to leave. Each time we prepared to call his owner to take him home, Rocky’s condition worsened again. 💔

It remains a bit of a mystery what exactly is going on inside this little body, and whether or when he will ever be well enough to go home. What we do know is that Rocky is a very special puppy. He is gentle, patient, and friendly with all the other dogs at the clinic, and he faces every up and down with quiet resilience.

Only time will tell what the future holds for Rocky, but one thing is certain: we will not give up on him. 💛

WAZIRI MKUU, Dkt. Mwigulu Nchemba amezitaka wizara zinazohusika na masuala ya ajira zisimamie kikamilifu utekelezaji wa sheria zinazotaka kazi zinazoweza kufanywa na Watanzania zisifanywe na wageni isipokuwa zile zinazohitaji utaalamu ambao nchi inaupungufu.
 
Vilevile, Waziri Mkuu amekemea tabia ya baadhi ya wenye nyumba kumpangisha raia mmoja wa kigeni na kumruhusu mpangaji huyo apangishe watu wengine ndani ya nyumba hiyo jambo ambalo ni hatari kwa usalama na pia halina tija kibiashara.
 
Mheshimiwa Dkt. Mwigulu ametoa agizo hilo leo Jumatano, Januari 14, 2026 alipofungua Kikao cha Mawaziri, Naibu Mawaziri, Makatibu Wakuu na Manaibu Makatibu Wakuu wa Wizara za Kisekta kujadili fursa za ajira ndani na nje ya nchi.
 
Agizo hilo linalenga kuongeza fursa za ajira kwa Watanzania kufuatia kuwepo kwa wimbi kubwa la wageni kufanya kazi au biashara ambazo zinaweza kufanywa na Watanzania na kuliwezesha Taifa kukabiliana na changamoto ya upungufu wa ajira.
 
“…Kazi zinazoweza kufanywa na Watanzania ziachwe wafanye, si kuruhusu wageni wafanye. Tusioneane aibu kama tumefungua milango au kulegeza wataalamu wafuatilie. Wageni wafanye kazi za kitaalamu ambazo nchi ina uhaba wa wataalamu.”
 
Amesema kuwa ni lazima wataalamu wa ndani wasimamie sheria ipasavyo na kama kuna maeneo yanayokwamisha wayabainishe na yafanyiwe marekebisho. “Hatuwezi kuleta watu wanaokuja kufanya kazi ambazo Watazania wanaziweza.”
 
Katika hatua nyingine, Mheshimiwa Dkt. Mwigulu ametoa wito kwa Watanzania kuwa na wivu na nchi yao kwa kutoruhusu baadhi ya vitu kufanyika, ambapo alitolea mfano suala la wenye nyumba kumpangisha raia moja wa kigeni ambaye naye analeta wenzake wengi katika nyumba hiyo hiyo.
 
“Watanzania tuwe na wivu na nchi yetu, mfano mtu anamkodishia nyumba mgeni kwa dola 5,000 kwa mwaka na kisha mgeni huyo anawaleta wenzake 60 na anawakodisha dola 500 hapo Mtanzania anapata hasara, hii si sawa hata kwa usalama.”
 
Waziri Mkuu amewaagiza wahusika wafuatilie suala hilo la makazi ili wakae katika utaratibu ulio rasmi. “Eneo hili liangaliwe wageni wanalundikana na kufanya kazi ambazo Watanzania wangeweza kufanya, hatuwezi kuruhusu hili tunataka wawekezaji.”
 
Hivyo, Waziri Mkuu ameziagiza wizara zinazohusika zifuatilie suala hilo, pamoja na kuwasisitiza wasimamie utekelezwaji wa sheria kwa sababu kila nchi ina sheria zake na Tanzania inatekeleza majukumu yake kwa kufuata sheria.
 
Amesema sheria zimetungwa ili kusaidia kujenga kampuni za Watanzania na kuzikuza, hivyo wizara zinazohusika zihakikishe hazisajili kampuni za kigeni kabla ya kuzifanyia uchunguzi wa kina kwa sababu baadhi ya taarifa zinazowasilishwa si sahihi.

My Bully Laughed as He Pushed Me Toward the Speeding Car—Until My Dog Took the Hit Meant for Me.

Chapter 1: The Weight of Gold

The afternoon sun in Oak Ridge, Connecticut, has a way of making everything look like a postcard. The white picket fences, the manicured lawns, the way the light filters through the ancient oaks—it’s the kind of place people move to when they want to believe nothing bad can ever happen.

But I knew better. Bad things happened in the shadows of those oaks every single day.

My name is Leo Miller. I’m sixteen, and my superpower is being invisible. I’ve mastered the art of walking close to the walls in the hallway, of keeping my head down during lunch, and of never, ever making eye contact with anyone who looks like they have something to prove.

It’s a lonely way to live, but it’s safe. Or at least, it was.

The only person—well, creature—who truly saw me was Buddy.

We got Buddy from the shelter when I was nine. My dad had just walked out for the third and final time, and my mom, Sarah, decided that if there wasn't going to be a man in the house, there should at least be a protector. Buddy wasn't much of a protector back then; he was a goofy ball of golden fur who tripped over his own paws and had a strange obsession with eating my socks.

But as the years went by, we grew into each other. When my stutter got so bad in seventh grade that I stopped talking to people entirely, I talked to Buddy. I read him my English essays. I told him about the girls I liked but would never talk to. I told him about the way my chest felt tight every time I walked past the gym.

Buddy just listened. He’d rest his heavy head on my knee, his brown eyes full of a wisdom that seemed older than the town itself. He was my anchor.

Today started like any other Tuesday. The air was thick with the scent of freshly cut grass and the looming threat of the chemistry final I was definitely going to fail.

I was walking Buddy along Elm Street, heading toward the small park near our duplex. Buddy was in high spirits, his tail wagging a rhythmic thwack-thwack against my leg. He was seven now, a little slower, a little grayer around the muzzle, but still as loyal as a heartbeat.

"Almost there, Bud," I murmured. "Then you can chase the squirrels."

Then I heard the roar of an engine.

I didn't have to look to know who it was. Tyler Vance’s silver Silverado was as much a part of the local ecosystem as the oaks. Tyler was the crown prince of Oak Ridge High. Captain of the football team, son of the town’s most successful real estate mogul, and possessor of a smile that could charm the stripes off a tiger.

He was also a predator.

He didn't pick on everyone. Just the ones who couldn't fight back. The ones who didn't have a father at home to call his father. The ones like me.

The truck swerved toward the curb, tires chirping as he braked hard. Tyler leaned out the window, his golden-boy hair perfectly tousled.

"Miller! Hey, Miller!"

I kept walking. Don't look back. Don't engage. Just keep moving.

"I'm talking to you, Stutter-Boy!"

Buddy stopped, his ears perking up. He sensed my heart rate spike. He stepped between me and the truck, a silent guardian.

Tyler jumped out of the driver's seat, followed by Marcus and Jax. They were the lieutenants—boys who traded their dignity for the reflected glory of Tyler’s popularity. Marcus already had his phone out, the lens pointed at me like a weapon.

"What do you want, Tyler?" I asked, the words catching in my throat. I hated how my voice betrayed me.

"Just a chat, Leo. Why so tense?" Tyler stepped into my personal space. He was a head taller than me and twice as broad. He smelled like expensive detergent and a life without consequences.

"I'm... I'm busy. Taking the dog out."

Tyler looked down at Buddy. "That's a lot of dog for a little guy like you. What’s his name? Scrap? Trash?"

"His name is Buddy," I said, my grip tightening on the leash.

"Buddy. Creative. Suits you." Tyler reached out to pat Buddy’s head, but Buddy pulled back, a low, guttural vibration starting in his chest.

Tyler’s face darkened. He didn't like things that didn't obey him. "Watch your mutt, Miller. Or maybe the city should watch him for you. I hear the pound is looking for 'aggressive' animals."

"He's not aggressive," I snapped, a sudden spark of anger overcoming my fear. "He just doesn't like you."

The silence that followed was heavy. Marcus and Jax looked at each other, grinning. They knew Tyler wouldn't let that slide.

"Is that right?" Tyler took a step forward, forcing me back toward the edge of the street. "Well, I don't much like him either. Or you."

He started the "game." It was a series of small shoves. Just enough to keep me off balance.

"Hey, look at him stumble!" Jax laughed.

"Give us a speech, Leo," Marcus mocked. "T-t-t-tell us how you r-r-really feel."

I felt the heat rising in my face. The humiliation was a familiar weight, but today, with Buddy there, it felt sharper. Buddy was agitated now, dancing on his paws, his eyes darting between the three boys. He wanted to help me, but he was waiting for my command.

"Leave us alone," I said, my voice finally clear. "Please."

"Make me," Tyler challenged.

We were at the corner of Elm and Maple. The afternoon traffic was picking up. I could hear the hum of cars in the distance.

"One more step, Miller," Tyler said, his eyes dancing with a cruel light. "Let's see if you can fly."

I looked behind me. The street was wide, and a black SUV was coming down the incline. It was moving fast—too fast for a residential zone.

"Tyler, stop. There’s a car."

"A car? Oh no, I'm so scared!" Tyler laughed. He looked at Marcus’s phone, performing for the camera. "Did you hear that, guys? Leo thinks a car is gonna save him."

He lunged.

It wasn't a playful shove. It was a full-force, two-handed strike to my chest. He used his entire weight, the frustration of his own hidden pressures—his demanding father, the scouts watching his every move, the fear of not being enough—all channeled into that one moment of violence.

I felt my feet leave the ground.

Time did that thing it does in movies—it stretched and warped. I saw the blue sky, the green leaves of the oaks, and then, the terrifyingly close grill of the SUV. I saw the driver’s face, a woman with blonde hair, her mouth open in a silent scream as she slammed on her brakes.

I felt the leash slip from my hand.

I hit the asphalt, the impact jarring my teeth. I closed my eyes, waiting for the end. I thought of my mom, how she’d have to identify me. I thought of my unfinished chemistry homework.

Then, something slammed into me.

It wasn't the car. It was warm, fur-covered, and solid.

Buddy.

He had sensed it before it happened. The moment the leash went slack, he didn't run for the sidewalk. He didn't run for safety. He launched himself into the path of the car to reach me.

His body hit mine like a cannonball, propelling me across the lane, toward the far gutter.

Then came the sound.

CRUNCH-THUD.

The SUV swerved, its tires screaming as they tore into the road. It missed me by inches.

I rolled into the gutter, my head spinning. For a second, I thought I was okay. I thought we were both okay.

"Buddy?" I wheezed, pushing myself up.

The SUV had stopped. The driver was out, screaming.

But I only had eyes for the middle of the street.

There was a heap of golden fur lying on the blacktop. He wasn't moving. A dark, visceral red began to spread from beneath him, staining the pristine suburban street.

"No," I whispered. It was a prayer and a protest. "No, Buddy. No."

I ran to him. I didn't see the neighbors coming out. I didn't see Tyler, standing frozen on the sidewalk. I only saw my best friend.

I knelt in the blood, cradling his head. He was breathing, but it was a wet, struggling sound. His beautiful golden coat was torn, and his back legs were twisted at an angle that made my stomach flip.

"I'm here, Buddy. I'm here." I sobbed, stroking his ears.

His eyes found mine. They were dimming, the light fading like a sunset, but he recognized me. He let out a tiny, soft whimper. He wasn't asking for help; he was checking on me.

On the sidewalk, the laughter had vanished as if it had never existed.

Tyler Vance looked like a statue of a ghost. His hands were shaking. He looked at the blood on the road, then at me, then at the neighbors who were already pointing and shouting his name.

"I... I just..." Tyler’s voice was a high, thin reed. "It was just a joke, Leo. I swear to God, I didn't mean... I didn't see the car..."

"He saved me," I said, my voice flat and dead. I didn't even look at him. "He saved me from you."

Tyler let out a sound—a choked, gutteral sob that came from deep in his chest. He turned and threw up in the grass. Then he fell to his knees, burying his face in his hands, the realization of what his "joke" had cost finally breaking through the armor of his privilege.

But his regret didn't mean anything. It couldn't put Buddy back together.

I felt Buddy’s body go limp in my arms. The tail thumped once. Twice.

Then, silence.

The most loyal soul I had ever known was gone, and the boy who killed him was crying on the sidewalk.

Greenland ndicho kisiwa kikubwa zaidi duniani kisicho bara.

3. Nchi Inayojitawala Ndani ya Denmark. Greenland ni nchi inayojitawala ndani ya Ufalme wa Denmark. Ilipata Home Rule mwaka 1979 na Self Rule mwaka 2009. Inaendelea kuchukua majukumu zaidi ya kujitawala taratibu.

4. Historia ya Zaidi ya Miaka 4,500. Binadamu waliwasili Greenland karibu mwaka 2500 KK. Waviking waliishi kusini lakini walitoweka karne ya 15. Inuit ndio waliobaki na kizazi chao kinaishi hadi leo.

Maneno kama “kayak” na “igloo” yametoka Greenlandic.

8. Uvuvi na Uwindaji wa Baharini. Uvuvi ni sekta muhimu sana ya uchumi. Kuna mgao maalum wa samaki, nyangumi na sili. Nyama ya nyangumi na sili huliwa ndani ya nchi tu.

9. Jiji Kuu lenye Maisha Hai. Takriban robo ya wakazi wanaishi Nuuk. Lina makumbusho, mikahawa na vituo vya sanaa. Limezungukwa na milima na fjordi nzuri.

10. Jua Lisilozama (Midnight Sun) Kuanzia Mei 25 hadi Julai 25 jua halizami. Juni 21 ni siku ndefu zaidi na sikukuu ya taifa.

1 cup of turkey berry.

2 handful sweet basil.
5 red chili,Cut diagonally for garnishing.

1 cup of coconut cream.
4 cup of coconut milk.

Instructions:

- Wait for it to boil again, add sweet basil leaves and turn off the heat immediately.
- Scoop into bowl. Ready to serve.
